key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% at six months but does not significantly reduce debt, and it lowers autopay enrollment overall, increasing missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts, six-month follow-up on payment behavior and autopay enrollment.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's central worry: a choice-architecture change can move a nominal enrollment/behavior metric while leaving the real outcome (amount paid down / saved) unchanged, and can have side effects (missed payments) among liquidity-constrained users — exactly the disengagement/harm pattern the support team is worried about for round-up savings.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not a savings product
US context, not EU
does not test opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment directly, only a shrouding nudge within autopay settings
relevance_reason: Consumer financial self-directed setting showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behavior without changing the real outcome, contradicting the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: Synthesizes decades of DC plan research, noting automatic enrollment and default investment options raise participation but can carry negative long-term effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative overview/state-of-the-art review of DC plan design literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a recent (2024) synthesis of the engagement-cost side of default enrollment that the support team's objection echoes, useful context even though the mechanism is employer-mediated.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
narrative overview rather than a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
US regulatory and tax context (SECURE 2.0) doesn't transfer to EU consumer product
relevance_reason: Recent overview of default effects and engagement costs in the closest analogous literature (employer retirement plans).

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces passivity (low contribution rates, non-management, account churn) that undermines long-term welfare gains unless paired with auto-escalation and re-enrollment prompts.
methodology: Policy discussion article synthesizing prior empirical findings. Abstract-only, no new data.
why_it_matters: States plainly the mechanism the support team fears (passive enrollment without engagement) and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, reminders) that are directly transferable design ideas for the round-up feature.
limitations: US retirement system focus, not consumer savings
opinion/policy piece, not primary empirical evidence
zero citations, unclear rigor
relevance_reason: Explicitly frames the passivity-vs-participation trade-off the brief asks about, with concrete mitigation ideas.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and theoretical framework for downstream (long-run) default effects, showing they depend on the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and sets a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent findings.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework paper drawing on the consumer-behavior default literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured lens for exactly the persistence question the brief asks — which conditions make a default's effect last vs fade — and should shape what the team measures at 6-12 months rather than just enrollment at day one.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual rather than a specific quantitative effect size
not focused on financial products specifically
no primary data of its own
relevance_reason: A 2025 consumer-behavior framework directly organizing the downstream-persistence question central to the enrolment-design decision.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization even for low-income beneficiaries, and passivity is highly insensitive to the value of the default option; variation in active choice appears driven by transitory attention shocks, not stable attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random/quasi-random assignment to default options in a large administrative health-insurance dataset.
why_it_matters: Shows defaults can 'stick' even when clearly costly to the passive chooser, a caution against assuming default-driven enrollment is welfare-neutral; also informs how to interpret who is and isn't attentive when comparing active choice to defaults.
limitations: government health-insurance enrollment, not a consumer financial/savings product
low-income Medicare population differs from the app's user base
no direct measure of amount saved/withdrawn
relevance_reason: Strong natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and passivity insensitivity, useful analogy despite a different domain.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6 percentage points from automatic enrollment and 0.3 points from default auto-escalation once job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-outs from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of those defaulted into auto-escalation actually escalate on the first date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative-data analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrollment gains shrink substantially once medium/long-run dynamics (withdrawal, opt-out, turnover) are modeled — directly bears on whether an opt-out round-up default would be vanity enrollment.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated turnover/vesting dynamics don't map onto a banking app
no EU or fintech context
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment reliably lifts real savings once realistic attrition dynamics are modeled.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrolled individuals actively opted back out; the default effect was stronger when incentives were higher and among people who didn't know their enrollment status.
methodology: Quasi-experimental evaluation of a nationwide policy using linked administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Quantifies exactly the kind of headline enrollment-lift number the internal argument is citing (23pp), while also showing most of that lift reverses via active opt-out — a caution against reading gross enrollment as durable.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension, not a consumer savings app
low-income employee population may not match the app's users
no data on amount saved or persistence beyond opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Recent large-scale default-enrollment natural experiment with an explicit enrollment effect size and opt-out reversal, close in spirit to the enrollment-vanity question.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings increases though inequality in savings falls; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete medium-run (36-month) horizon on default persistence and separates the enrollment effect from the amount-saved effect and distributional (inequality) effect — precisely the three questions the brief poses, even though the setting is pensions.
limitations: retirement savings, not liquid consumer savings
employer/national pension systems, not a fintech app
structural model's switching-cost estimate may not transfer to a low-friction app setting
relevance_reason: Recent, methodologically strong evidence separating short vs medium-run default persistence and distributional effects, directly answering the brief's persistence question by analogy.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person five-European-country sample, default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one people refuse) lowers ratings of the advisor's advice, an effect also of medium-to-large size, mediated by perceived honesty.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, manipulating default presence and framing in investment/risk allocation decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the reputational/manipulation risk the brief flags: a default that shifts behavior can simultaneously erode trust in the institution presenting it, which should shape how the round-up default and any pre-selected multiplier are framed and communicated in the EU app.
limitations: wealth-manager advisory context rather than a self-serve banking app
risk-taking/investment allocation, not a round-up savings mechanism
does not report persistence beyond the immediate experimental session
relevance_reason: EU multi-country experimental evidence on when a default reads as helpful vs manipulative, directly informing the dark-pattern risk the brief cares about.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants anchored on the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default rate/fund after three years; the participation gain and the anchoring loss roughly offset in average asset accumulation, though the lower tail of the savings distribution improves.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset default level anchors most people who would otherwise have chosen differently — the core evidence the field still argues with on the anchoring question this project needs answered for the multiplier decision.
limitations: classic pension study, predates fintech/app context and current EU regulatory climate
employer-mediated trust mechanism doesn't carry to a self-directed app
no year given, suggesting an older/foundational working paper rather than current evidence
relevance_reason: The classic result on default-level anchoring that the brief explicitly flags as needing updated, non-pension confirmation.

key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together (removing either alone collapses adherence), and adding an intermediate preset option (15% alongside 20/25/30%) captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records, validated against an independent stated-preference survey of tipping preferences, with counterfactual menu simulations.
why_it_matters: The structural decomposition of why people accept preset menu options and the counterfactual analysis of adding an intermediate preset level transfers directly to the multiplier decision: it gives a method for testing whether adding a 2x-style intermediate option between 1x and 5x would capture most of the achievable benefit without the extremes.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings or financial contributions
US taxi context, not EU or banking
welfare/counterfactual framework assumes a stated-preference benchmark that a savings-pot analogue would need to replicate
relevance_reason: Explicit structural-modeling and counterfactual-menu-design method that transfers to deciding whether and where to pre-set the round-up multiplier.

key_finding: In an opt-in short-term (liquid, withdrawable-anytime) payroll savings program at five UK firms, no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of program administrative data from five U.K. employers over a 12-month activation window.
why_it_matters: The closest available product analog to a liquid round-up savings pot: shows opt-in enrollment yields very low take-up but the enrolled minority is highly persistent and engaged — direct evidence for the 'active choice gets the engaged users without the disengagement cost' question, though not the 'employer as trusted intermediary' mechanism.
limitations: employer payroll deduction context, not a standalone consumer banking app
does not test opt-out or active-choice designs, only opt-in
UK-specific, sample restricted to employees who stayed employed 12 months
relevance_reason: Directly studies a liquid, withdrawable short-term savings product under opt-in, the nearest real product analog to the round-up feature.

key_finding: Characterizes when opt-out minimization versus maximization is the asymptotically optimal default design, showing that simple weighted opt-out minimization is optimal when the designer and choosers agree on the activity's value, with extensions for externalities, fees, and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical welfare-economics model of optimal default design, validated with numerical simulations. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative decision rule — when designer and user preferences are aligned, minimize the effort to opt out (i.e., a helpful opt-out default is justified); when they diverge, caution against defaulting people in, which is exactly the ethical line the brief wants drawn between helpful and manipulative design.
limitations: purely theoretical/asymptotic result, not tested empirically in any product setting
no named population or context to compare against the app's users
assumes stylized value-agreement structure that a real product would need to validate
relevance_reason: General normative framework for when an opt-out default is justified versus manipulative, directly relevant to the entry-design ethics question.

key_finding: EU dark-pattern law is best understood as protecting consumer autonomy, and the article develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations for assessing choice-architecture practices like pre-selected defaults.
methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis mapping EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only, no empirical measurement.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal taxonomy for judging whether an opt-out default or pre-set multiplier reads as manipulative, directly informing how to keep the entry design on the right side of dark-pattern regulation.
limitations: doctrinal/legal analysis, not empirical evidence of behavioral effect
no data on enrolment or savings outcomes
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk concern for whatever entry design is chosen.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, only 25% of employees opted out within 12 months (versus roughly 50% opt-out at lower defaults per prior literature), and non-opters ended up at a suboptimal contribution level anchored to the default.
methodology: Observational analysis of a single employer retirement plan's administrative records, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
why_it_matters: Shows a preset level can anchor people at a suboptimal rate rather than what they would otherwise choose, directly bearing on the risk of pre-selecting a round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
matched-contribution incentive structure doesn't apply to round-up savings
relevance_reason: Strong anchoring evidence for the preset-multiplier decision, by analogy from the closest adjacent literature.

key_finding: Abstract text unavailable; title indicates field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings across four large U.K. programs.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to involve large-scale field experiments per the title.
why_it_matters: Short-term, non-pension automated savings experiments could be a close analogue to round-up savings, but no findings can be extracted from the available text.
limitations: abstract text is corrupted/missing so no verifiable findings
still payroll-mediated rather than a self-directed consumer app
relevance_reason: Title suggests high relevance (short-term automated savings) but content cannot be assessed from the available abstract.

key_finding: At-scale field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though alerts captured less than half of potential avoidable savings.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks measuring downstream financial outcomes of an auto-enrolled consumer banking feature.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that auto-enrollment into a passive banking-app feature can produce real, measurable financial benefit at scale, closely analogous to auto-enrolling users into round-up savings, while showing defaults capture only partial potential benefit.
limitations: measures overdraft alerts, not a savings-level enrolment decision
no comparison of opt-in vs opt-out vs active-choice enrolment designs
relevance_reason: Closest real-world UK consumer-banking-app auto-enrolment evidence, directly analogous to the round-up feature's Entry decision.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment increases savings by £32-38/month but is partially offset by £7/month more unsecured debt over 41 months, alongside modest increases in mortgage uptake and improved credit scores.
methodology: Large-scale randomized roll-out of UK auto-enrollment pensions across roughly 160,000 small employers, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Shows that nominal savings gains from auto-enrollment can be partially offset by other financial behavior, cautioning against treating enrolment or headline savings figures as the whole welfare picture for a liquid round-up product.
limitations: employer pension context, not a liquid consumer savings app
debt-offset mechanism may not transfer to small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Evidence that automatic enrolment's savings gains are not a pure win, informing how to measure true benefit rather than nominal enrolment.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrolment 'ordeal' (removing auto-enrollment) to health insurance reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment analyzing removal of an auto-enrollment policy in health insurance, supported by a theoretical adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how large an enrolment drop a friction/opt-in step can cause and shows it falls hardest on people least equipped to actively opt in, a distributional warning relevant to choosing opt-in or active choice over opt-out.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a savings product
adverse-selection dynamics are specific to insurance markets
relevance_reason: Strong effect-size and distributional evidence on how much friction depresses enrolment and who it hurts, relevant by analogy to the Entry decision.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who likely did not intend recurring commitments.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites around the 2020 U.S. election.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that a pre-checked recurring-commitment default can produce complaints and regret, and disproportionately affects inexperienced users -- the exact 'nominal enrolment, real regret' risk the support team is warning about for round-up savings.
limitations: political donations, not a financial savings product
US context, not EU consumer-protection regime
relevance_reason: Best available quantified evidence of default-driven regret/complaints and distributional harm, directly supporting the request for contradicting evidence.

key_finding: In a search model and experiment, a default raises the reservation utility (reference effect) and induces self-selection, so those who reject the default and search actively tend to find better options.
methodology: Laboratory experiment testing a reference-dependent search-cost model.
why_it_matters: Suggests users who override a default are self-selected toward better choices, a nuance for interpreting who benefits from a preset multiplier versus an empty field.
limitations: abstract-only, generic lab search task, not a financial or consumer-app setting
no direct measure of enrolment or savings amount
relevance_reason: Provides a theoretical/experimental mechanism for self-selection around defaults, tangential to the anchoring question.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting at least 15 months and differing by rollout scope.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered EU DMA choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The clearest recent, EU-regulatory-context evidence that a mandated active-choice screen produces large, durable shifts away from a preset default, directly informing whether active choice can substitute for opt-out in the Entry decision.
limitations: studies browser choice, not a financial product
effect size may depend on rollout mechanics (new vs. existing devices) that may not transfer
relevance_reason: Best available EU, at-scale, persistence-tracked comparison of active choice against defaults, central to the Entry decision.

key_finding: In a usability study of 410 participants, generalizable opt-out privacy interfaces (letting one choice apply broadly) slightly reduced opt-out utility but substantially increased efficiency and reduced disruption, with the least disruptive scheme leaving 98% of participants feeling undisrupted.
methodology: Design and usability study of nine privacy opt-out interface schemes implemented as a browser extension.
why_it_matters: Shows how to design a no-default, active-choice interface that feels non-disruptive rather than manipulative, informing how an active-choice flow for round-up enrolment could be built without annoying users.
limitations: privacy-consent context (CCPA/GPC), not financial savings
US regulatory setting rather than EU
relevance_reason: Offers interface-design lessons for making an active-choice/no-default flow usable and non-disruptive, relevant to the active-choice option.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults for university exam sign-up increased sign-up uptake, but for the effortful outcome (actually passing the exam) gains appeared only for a single exam with a strongly-endorsed default and only among students previously responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed higher sign-up but no gain in actual completion.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out across two university study programs.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the core disengagement risk the brief asks about: an opt-out default can inflate nominal enrolment while doing nothing for the effortful, real outcome for the people it doesn't fit -- precisely the support team's concern about passively-enrolled users who don't engage.
limitations: university exam context, not a financial product
small-scale, single-institution setting
relevance_reason: The closest available evidence that a default can raise sign-up numbers without producing real behavior change for a subset of users, central to the nominal-vs-real-engagement question.

key_finding: After target-date funds became a permissible default investment option, younger workers' equity share rose and older workers' fell, tracking the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. middle-class investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly reshape a downstream parameter (allocation) while barely moving the level/contribution decision itself, a caution that a preset round-up multiplier may anchor the amount less than expected.
limitations: employer retirement plan context, portfolio allocation rather than a savings-level decision
US pension-specific policy driver doesn't apply to consumer apps
relevance_reason: Evidence that defaults can fail to move the specific 'level' parameter analogous to the round-up multiplier, informing the anchoring question.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, behavioral nudges including default options significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China, with the largest backfire effects from positive-narrative and default-option nudges, and heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Direct empirical contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise, showing a default option can backfire and reduce contributions, with important heterogeneity -- exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked to be represented.
limitations: small survey-based sample (n=220), not a real behavioral/field measure
Chinese voluntary pension context, culturally and institutionally different from an EU consumer banking app
relevance_reason: Provides the explicit contradicting evidence the brief requested that defaults may reduce rather than increase desired financial behavior.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, financial nudges framed around savings and targeting deliberate (System 2) decision-making were rated most favourably, with transparency having no significant effect on approval or perceived manipulation.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment; 36 hypothetical financial intervention scenarios; representative sample of 2,100 Australians; six dependent variables including approval and manipulation.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern reputational risk named in the brief: shows how framing (savings vs spending) and messenger (bank) affect whether a nudge is perceived as helpful or manipulative, which should shape the messaging around whichever entry design is chosen.
limitations: Hypothetical vignettes rather than actual enrolment behaviour
Australian sample, not the EU regulatory context named in the brief
No measurement of enrolment, persistence, or amount saved
relevance_reason: Tests perceived manipulation and approval of financial nudges, which is the dark-pattern risk criterion the brief explicitly flags.

key_finding: Offering conditional cash transfer recipients a bank-account delivery option produced no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances among those with previously nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment on delivery-channel choice for conditional cash transfers; comparison of cash vs bank-account deposit; downstream asset and trust measures.
why_it_matters: Shows that giving people a savings-account channel only moves the needle for the least-saving subgroup, a distributional pattern relevant to who benefits from any enrolment design, but the CCT/low-income setting is far from a self-directed banking-app user.
limitations: Population is low-income CCT beneficiaries, not consumer banking-app users
Not an opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment comparison
No multi-month persistence data on amounts saved
relevance_reason: Marginally informative on heterogeneous savings response to account-based interventions, but not a direct test of enrolment defaults.

key_finding: Contribution amounts and liquid-fund availability are described as identical across compared program cases, based on the fragment available.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to compare automatic-IRA program variants including an emergency-savings (liquid) component.
why_it_matters: If it reports enrolment or withdrawal data for a liquid, auto-enrolled savings component alongside a retirement account, it could speak to whether liquidity changes default effects, but the fragment gives no usable numbers.
limitations: Abstract is a single fragmentary sentence, not a usable summary
Auto-IRA is a state/employer-adjacent program, not a self-directed consumer app
No effect sizes or persistence data visible
relevance_reason: Touches on a liquid-savings sidecar to automatic enrolment, conceptually close to round-up savings, but the available text is too thin to extract findings.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment with a default contribution rate and fund allocation dramatically raised participation, and a large share of employees stuck to both defaults years later, evidence of a 'power of suggestion' effect.
methodology: Natural experiment: before/after analysis of one large US corporation's switch from opt-in to automatic 401(k) enrolment, administrative plan data.
why_it_matters: One of the two founding studies of the default-effect literature the whole field argues with; establishes both the enrolment lift and the anchoring-on-default-rate phenomenon (directly analogous to the round-up multiplier decision) but in an employer-mediated plan.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app the user chose to download
Single-firm before/after design, not a randomized comparison
No consumer-liquidity or withdrawal-behaviour data
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for both the default-effect-on-enrolment and anchoring-on-preset-level questions the brief asks about, though in an employer setting the brief says doesn't carry over directly.

key_finding: No usable finding is stated; the record provides only a title comparing savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrolment in a defined-contribution plan.
methodology: abstract-only; no abstract text available.
why_it_matters: If it compares auto- vs voluntary-enrolment savings behaviour with effect sizes it would bear on C1, but nothing in the record can currently support that.
limitations: No abstract available to assess claims or methodology
Defined-contribution retirement plan setting, not a consumer banking app
Cannot verify sample, design, or effect sizes
relevance_reason: Title suggests a direct auto- vs voluntary-enrolment comparison, but the missing abstract leaves nothing to evaluate.

key_finding: Across three representative Estonian surveys, low trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status were both associated with under-saving and with early withdrawal of retirement savings after a pension-freedom reform.
methodology: Analysis of three nationally representative surveys (2020-2022) around an Estonian pension-freedom reform introducing early withdrawal.
why_it_matters: Directly speaks to the support team's worry that passively-enrolled, disengaged users disproportionately withdraw quickly: shows that specific subgroups (low institutional trust, minority status) are the ones most likely to both under-save and pull money out, which should shape who any enrolment default is expected to help or hurt.
limitations: Mandatory pension savings scheme, not a self-directed consumer app
Withdrawal behaviour studied around a policy reform, not around enrolment-design choice itself
Estonian institutional-trust context may not generalize to the EU banking-app user base
relevance_reason: Gives distributional evidence on who under-saves and withdraws early, matching the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt by passive enrolment.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent survey experiment across G7 countries, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrolment vaccination policy reduced their stated intentions and did not increase, and sometimes decreased, approval of the policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment (n=24,303) across G7 countries testing reflection on a hypothetical default-enrolment policy.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults quietly and costlessly raise uptake: when people are prompted to notice they were defaulted in, both stated behavioural intentions and policy approval can fall, a backlash risk directly relevant to how the round-up opt-out flow is disclosed under EU consumer-protection scrutiny.
limitations: Vaccination/health-policy setting, not a financial product
Stated intentions in a hypothetical scenario, not observed financial enrolment or savings behaviour
No consumer-app or self-directed-finance population studied
relevance_reason: Provides a rare finding that reflecting on a default can backfire and reduce support, a direct challenge to the 'defaults always help' premise the brief wants tested, even though the domain is health rather than finance.

key_finding: Using FINRA's 2018 Millennial Investment Study, automatic enrolment and employer-matching provisions were associated with higher likelihood of retirement-plan participation among Millennials.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis of US Millennials' retirement-plan participation, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Replicates the well-established default-effect finding in a more recent cohort, but adds nothing new about persistence, anchoring, or active choice, and the employer-plan mechanism does not transfer to a self-directed app.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer banking app
Cross-sectional survey data, not a randomized or natural-experiment design
Employer match is conflated with automatic enrolment, confounding the default effect
relevance_reason: Confirms the default-effect direction in a contemporary sample but is largely redundant with older, more rigorous employer-plan studies already in this set.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations on Danish savers, each $1 of subsidy spending (an active-choice-driven policy) raised total saving by only 1 cent, while automatic employer contributions (a default) substantially raised wealth accumulation, because 85% of savers are 'passive' and unresponsive to active-choice incentives.
methodology: Population-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings, decomposing responses to active (subsidy) versus passive (automatic contribution) policy changes.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the argument that active choice captures most of the benefit of a default: shows the large majority of people simply do not respond to an active-choice mechanism, while automatic/default contributions move nearly everyone, a strong quantitative counterweight for the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged savings accounts, not a liquid consumer round-up product
Automatic contributions here are employer-administered, the intermediary mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
No engagement, withdrawal, or complaint data for the passively-enrolled group
relevance_reason: The strongest quantitative evidence available on active-choice versus default policy effectiveness, directly bearing on whether active choice can substitute for opt-out, though in a retirement-account setting.

key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — a forced-choice design that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option — as a way to nudge behaviour without a default, proposed as a complement or substitute when automatic enrolment is infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Review of prior active-choice applications (including savings) plus original studies including two field experiments testing standard and enhanced active choice.
why_it_matters: This is the specific mechanism the brief's active-choice question is asking about: the abstract explicitly frames active choice as an alternative to automatic (opt-out) enrolment for savings behaviour, and the 'enhanced' variant it proposes is a concrete design the round-up feature could adopt to get enrolment lift without full opt-out.
limitations: Field experiments reported are in a healthcare/medication-adherence context, not financial products
No amount-saved or multi-month persistence data reported
No direct comparison to opt-out enrolment on the same population
relevance_reason: The abstract explicitly names active choice as a savings-behaviour alternative to automatic enrolment and tests an enhanced version of it, which is the specific technique the brief's active-choice decision needs evidence on.

key_finding: A synthesis of household finance evidence showing that choice-architecture interventions, including defaults and product design, systematically shift financial behaviour across savings, borrowing, payments, and insurance, alongside the underlying behavioural mechanisms.
methodology: Narrative review/NBER chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and intervention evidence across household financial decisions.
why_it_matters: Serves as the review-of-effect-sizes the brief asks for: covers defaults and choice architecture across a wider range of self-directed consumer financial decisions than employer retirement plans alone, giving a broader base to calibrate expected default effect sizes for the round-up feature.
limitations: Narrative synthesis, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract-only detail on specific consumer round-up or fintech contexts
Much of the underlying evidence base is still retirement-plan literature
relevance_reason: A comprehensive review of behavioural household finance interventions including defaults and choice architecture, giving the effect-size synthesis the brief explicitly wants.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment pushed participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, with half still on the default rate and fund after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large US firms comparing automatic vs opt-in 401(k) enrolment over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The clearest classic demonstration that a preset default doesn't just lift enrolment but anchors the chosen level for years, directly informing the risk that a preset round-up multiplier will anchor most users at whatever level is pre-selected.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k) plan, not a self-directed consumer app
Default fund/rate is employer-chosen, not the multiplier-choice architecture in the brief
No data on disengagement, complaints, or withdrawal comparable to a liquid savings product
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for anchoring on preset default levels persisting for years, the exact mechanism the brief's round-up-multiplier decision worries about.

key_finding: Randomizing default enrolment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points, an effect equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings options; default assignment also made people more likely to actively choose to save afterward.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan, testing several default variants of a salary-linked savings account.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanistic explanation (present bias, cognitive cost) for why defaults work, and evidence that default exposure can build lasting saving habits, useful for interpreting whether a round-up default would similarly persist rather than just look good at signup.
limitations: Salary-linked account distributed via employer payroll, closer to the employer-intermediary mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
Developing-country labour-market context, not an EU consumer banking app
No data on amount saved or withdrawal at 6-12 months, only participation and attitudes
relevance_reason: Gives a rigorous randomized effect size for default enrolment and a mechanism (cognitive cost/present bias) that helps interpret why a round-up default might or might not persist, despite an employer-payroll setting.

key_finding: A randomized reminder nudge cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%; users with an overdraft history saw a net 5% increase in total fees while other users saved 15%.
methodology: Field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil randomizing payment reminders; abstract gives effect sizes on fee outcomes.
why_it_matters: Shows a behavioral nudge that looks beneficial on average can net-harm the exact vulnerable subgroup (those already prone to overdraft/liquidity strain) the support team worries about with passive enrolment, arguing the team should measure subgroup-level harm, not just aggregate enrolment, before defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment defaults
Brazilian credit-card and overdraft context differs from an EU round-up savings pot
no data on persistence beyond the experiment window
relevance_reason: Directly evidences the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk question (C5): a nudge helpful on average can systematically harm a subgroup, the failure mode the brief explicitly wants to avoid building.
